newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin aide suggests Russia could join NATO - agency.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin aide suggests Russia could join NATO - agency.

text.p: A top Kremlin security official said he favoured Russia joining NATO's political organisation and later even taking part in the military structures of the alliance, Interfax news agency said on Tuesday.

It was unclear whether the comments by Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin, who was appointed last month, was simply a personal opinion or reflected a change in Moscow's position, which has so far aimed at a separate bilateral treaty with NATO.
"Russia could sign an agreement on joining NATO's political structure," Interfax quoted Rybkin as saying in a magazine interview to be published on Wednesday.
"And then if it goes as we aim and as representatives of the Western states hope, we could join the military organisation," Rybkin told news weekly Itogi.

Russian officials, suspicious of NATO's plans to accept Moscow's former Cold War satellites in Eastern Europe, have ruled out seeking membership in the alliance. NATO officials have said there have been no such requests from Russia so far.
Russia has strongly opposed to NATO's plans to expand eastwards warning that this would raise tensions in Europe and make it consider unspecified counter-measures.
But as NATO has strengthened its committment to expand, Moscow has moved the focus of its efforts to striking a separate deal which would guarantee its security interests.
Rybkin said he favoured Russia following, in the initial stages, the example of France. For decades Paris remained a NATO member without submitting its forces to joint command.
He suggested that the time needed for Russia to apply for full membership was mainly limited to its ability to adjust its military structures to those of NATO.

"It's a different story how much time it will take to adapt our management and communisations systems," he said. "We can do this step by step starting from the counties with whom we take part in peacekeeping operations."
Russia has troops in Bosnia as part of NATO's peacekeeping force in the former Yugoslav republic.
It is also part of NATO's programme Partnership for Peace specially developed for setting up cooperation with non-members in Europe.
